D48 CRITICAL CARE CASE REPORTS: NEUROCRITICAL CARE, SEDATION, AND DELIRIUM  / Thematic Poster Session
Unable to Relax: A Case of Stiff Person Syndrome
W. Ning
1
, S. Iantorno
1
, C. Zhong
2
, S. Li
3
; 
1
Internal Medicine, LAC+USC Medical Center, Los
Angeles, CA, United States, 
2
Neurology, LAC+USC Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA, United
States, 
3
Pulmonary and Critical Care, LAC+USC Medical Center, Los Angeles, CA, United
States.
Introduction
 Stiff Person Syndrome (SPS) is an extremely rare and debilitating nervous system
disease that is presented with whole body stiffness, rigidity and spasms. This disease has an
estimated incidence of one case per million per year and therefore, not much information has
been written about this potentially devastating disease in which early diagnosis may be crucial to
prevent potential permanent and morbid consequences. 
Case Summary
 A 49 year old male with
history of recently diagnosed panic attacks and recurrent rhabdomyolysis presents after a panic
attack at home leading to cardiac arrest with return of spontaneous circulation. Labs were
significant for an elevated potassium to 9.1 mmol/L and creatinine kinase of up to 220,000 U/L.
The patient was intubated for airway protection and admitted to intensive care unit (ICU) for
further treatment. While in the ICU, patient underwent hypothermia protocol for preservation of
neurological function and continuous renal replacement therapy for rhabdomyolysis. Further
medical history was obtained from the family that was notable for the history of developing a
shooting pain and muscle spasms in his left leg 1.5 years ago that caused him to have difficulty
walking, leading him to fall down a flight of stairs and causing injury in his thoracic spine that
required surgical stabilization. After the surgery, family noted the patient to have hour long panic
attacks with muscle stiffness and spasms throughout his body, particularly in his core muscles.
The patient had seen a multitude of neurologists and was provided negative lab results and
imaging, without a specific diagnosis. Given the abnormal quality of the patient’s presentation, an
anti-GAD 65 was sent that returned elevated. The patient was diagnosed with Stiff Person
Syndrome and subsequently treated with diazepam. 
Discussion
 The proposed pathogenesis of
SPS is caused by the blockade of the inhibitory enzymes of the central nervous system, leading
to over-activation of the nervous system and causing the clinical presentation of uncontrollable
muscle stiffness and rigidity. Glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) is the enzyme responsible for
maintenance of neural inhibitory pathways and antibodies against the enzyme is responsible for
decline in level of gamma amino butyric acid (GABA), causing a loss in inhibitory mechanism for
the nervous system. Treatment include diazepam to assist in symptom management; however,
other treatments have been proposed such as steroids, plasmapheresis and intravenous
immunoglobulins but not much data has been gathered given the rarity of the disease.
